en: Sekoddeśapañjikā: Homage to the glorious Paramādibuddha.
Having bowed to Ādibuddha, the sole lord of the three realms of existence, together with the assembly of Bodhisattvas, Dharma, and Saṅgha,
[I write this] according to the instruction received from the feet of my glorious Guru.
I shall expand upon the introductory verses concerning initiation and the rest.

Then Sucandra, the emanation-body of Vajrapāṇi, spoke to the King for the sake of the consecration (*sekā*) in the *Paramādibuddha-tantrarāja*: "O Teacher, the consecration is of seven types, beginning with water and ending with the permission (*anujñā*).
There is another [set] of three types."
The sequence ends with the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*) of the vase (*kalaśa*).
"And likewise the unsurpassed" refers to the characteristic of the knowledge of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*).
"For the sake of mundane and supramundane accomplishments" means that mundane accomplishment extends as far as the Akaniṣṭha realm.
"And supramundane Buddhahood is the immutable gnosis of Mahāmudrā.
For this purpose, speak to me briefly.
"Listen," and so forth, is the speech of the Blessed One, continuing until the conclusion of the summary.
"Supreme" refers to the immutable gnosis of Mahāmudrā.
The "movement of the channels"— such as the left, right, and middle— refers to their coming and going through the left, right, and central apertures.
The movement through the channels and the breath-extension—this is prāṇāyāma;
I shall explain it to you according to its enumeration.
Now he states the divisions of the summary (uddeśa) and so forth:
"In every tantra, the summary is threefold;
likewise, the detailed exposition (nirdeśa) should be threefold."
He states the distinction between the summary (uddeśa) and the detailed exposition (nirdeśa):
"The sub-summary (pratyuddeśa) and the great summary (mahoddeśa)" is the division of the summary; "the sub-exposition (pratinirdeśaka) and the other" implies the great exposition (mahānirdeśa).
And these two are subdivisions of the exposition. He states their function [with the words] "In the exposition itself," and so forth.
That which is the summary (uddeśa) is itself the detailed exposition (nirdeśa),
and that is called the recitation of the tantra (tantra-saṃgīti).
For here, by the word "detailed exposition," the recitation of the extensive tantra (bṛhattantra-saṃgīti) is meant.
There is also a summary (*uddeśa*) contained within the great tantras;
for when that very [summary] is separated out by the compilers (*saṃgītikāraka*), it then becomes a separate tantra,
just as the *Anyatantrābhidhāna* emerged from the *Lakṣābhidhāna*.
And because of the word "ca" (and) in the phrase "pratyuddeśaś ca," when the word "prati" is implied, "pratinirdeśa" is stated;
these two are, respectively, the *Alpapañjikā* and the *Bṛhatpañjikā*.
And that [commentary] merely breaks down the words and does not indicate all meanings;

for it will be stated that the *ṭīkā* indicates all meanings. And because of the inclusion of the word "great" (*mahat*) from the wheel [of syllables], the term "Mahānirdeśa" (Great Exposition) is used.
These two are called, respectively, the *Alpaṭīkā* (the Short Commentary) and the *Bṛhaṭṭīkā* (the Great Commentary).

Thus, in the manner stated, by means of the six points (*ṣaṭkoṭi*)—the sixfold [categories] such as the recitation of the short and long tantras and so forth—the *Ādibuddha*, designated as the *Kālacakra*, shall be pure and completely purified;
this is the connection with what is to be explained hereafter.
"Thus, by the fourfold Vajrayogas" means by those characterized by the non-duality of mantra and form.
"By the four awakenings" means by the awakenings in a single moment, characterized by the fivefold and twentyfold awakenings of the *Māyājāla*.
[It refers to] the aggregates, characterized by form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
By means of the elements characterized as earth, water, fire, air, space, and the dharma-element;
by means of the twelve sense-bases through the relationship of object and subject;
and by means of those characterized as the dharma-elements of form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena.
By means of the six families characterized by the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
by the two truths, mundane and supramundane;
and through the complete purification of body, speech, and mind—there are two pairs of consecrations: the body is purified by the two [consecrations] of water and crown.
Purification of speech is through the silk ribbon and the vajra-bell;
purification of mind is through the great vow and the name;
and purification of gnosis is through the authorization.
Any other purification that exists is [attained] through the purification of the elements and so forth.
(40) Regarding this, he says: "Water," and so on.
"The vajra-bell is the great syllable" means that the vajra is purified by the great syllable.
The bell is the unceasing speech of the Buddha;
it is that very [speech] when the sun and moon are unified, characterized by the flow of the central channel (*madhyamā*).
However, the empowerments such as the water-pot (*kumbha*) and so forth may be bestowed even without the drawing of a mandala.
Because the attainment of bliss is perceived through the touch of the breasts and body;
"the progenitor of all Protectors" means he is the progenitor of the five Tathāgatas, the Protectors (*tāyin*), by virtue of their being free from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇatva*).
"Wisdom" (*prajñā*) is the intellect; its "images" (*bimba*) are characterized by the absence of the forms of subject and object, resembling an illusion or a dream, and are devoid of worldly desire.
Therefore he says: "by those who have transcended existence and non-existence," and so forth, including "non-existence.
For here, the object of cognition (*ālambana*) is of two kinds; it may be preceded by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

If it is preceded by inference, then that which is preceded by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—being free from the stain of all conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) due to the yoga of reality arising from the instructions of a true guru—appears like the circle of stars in the sky as a manifold *saṃbhogakāya*.
First, the practitioner at the stage of initial action perceives the entire universe with the fleshly eye, even without the superknowledges (*abhijñā*). (41)

Then, by means of the divine eye, through the power of the range of the superknowledges; then, by means of the Buddha-eye, through the power of the range of those free from passion; then, by means of the wisdom-eye, through the power of the range of the bodhisattvas.
Then, by means of the eye of wisdom (*jñānacakṣus*), through the power of the limit of a Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*) and because of liberation from all substrata (*upadhi*),
the five eyes of the Tathāgata— beginning with the flesh-eye and so forth— are thus described in relation to the vision of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

The conceptualization of the object of focus according to its true nature, preceded by inference, is like a painting displayed for beginners and practitioners; it is for the purpose of leading them onto the path of emptiness.

Therefore, when the image is non-existent—being similar to a dream and so forth—that cultivation which takes it as an object is not a conceptualization for yogins, because it arises from causes that are themselves beyond conceptual construction.
For this very reason, existence is the nature of the real thing.
And non-existence is characterized by the absence of all descriptive attributes;
since that which appears to the mind cannot be denied,
and because entities composed of atoms are not perceived, like a reflection.
He explains this very point by means of an illustration,
beginning with the words "pratisenām" (the reflected image).
By the word *pratisenā*, the object contemplated by another is denoted.
One should perceive that [vision] as being without substance in a mirror—that is, devoid of an aggregation of atoms.

Indeed, in the *Pratisenāvatāra-tantra*, the manifestation of the *pratisenā* is said to occur in eight [media]: the mirror, the sword, the thumb, the lamp, the moon, the sun, the water-vessel, and the eye.
Likewise, one perceives past and future phenomena contemplated within the sky. (42)
In the empty image containing all aspects, the yogi who has attained the path of non-conceptualization perceives [it].
As for the nature of this reflected image (*pratisenā*) while it is being seen—its characteristic of appearing—that is not a real entity; that object does not exist.
Why? He says:
"Because of the vision of an object devoid of a real entity (*vastu*). By "real entity" is meant an aggregate of atoms; it is "devoid" (*śūnya*), meaning it has been removed.

And that "object" (*artha*) of it is characterized by its appearance. "Because of the vision of that" means because of its apprehension through non-conceptual direct perception (*nirvikalpa-pratyakṣa*).
Since an object consisting of an aggregate of atoms does not exist, the referent exists as having the characteristic of a mental appearance.
How so? Just like an illusion, a dream, or a magical trick.
He states this very point:
"Non-existent," and so forth;

"like a wish-fulfilling gem," and so forth—this states that cognition is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*). [An objection is raised: "But how can that which is without an objective support (*anālambana*) accomplish the welfare of the world? For how could there be an arising without an object? To this he says:
"Non-seeing," and so forth.
The practitioners (*sādhaka*) are those who bring about the *pratisenā* [divination].
He says that even the view that "one sees a real form" is not correct.
He says "no" even to the claim that one sees a non-existent form;
this is expressed in the passage beginning with "yad api" (even that which...).
He also says "no" to the claim that one sees with the eyes of another.
"He does not see," and so forth.
To the question, "Then does he see with his own eyes?
he says, "With his own eyes," and so forth.
That which is being seen by the maiden as unborn and unarisen is her *jātaka* (birth-story), meaning it is as if it were arisen. He speaks of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*): "seen," and so forth.

When such a reflection, which resembles a dream or an illusion, has been seen, immediately thereafter one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*)—consisting of inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*)—continuously and without interruption.
To the question "In what [state]? he says:
"Upward," and so forth.
Above, there are three channels characterized by body, speech, and mind;
likewise below.
Among them, on the left is the lunar channel, characterized by the body.
In the south is the solar channel (*arkanāḍī*), which has the nature of speech;
in the center is the Rāhu channel (*rāhunāḍī*), which has the nature of mind;
and the feces channel (*viḍnāḍī*) has the nature of body.
The urine-channel has the nature of speech;
the semen-channel has the nature of mind;
the moon-channel has the nature of water.
The solar channel has the nature of fire;
the Rāhu channel has the nature of space;
the feces channel has the nature of earth.
The urine-channel has the nature of wind;
the semen-channel has the nature of gnosis.
This is what is expressed by the words beginning with "candra" and so forth.
"In the prāṇa and apāna respectively" means that the [first] three are in the prāṇa— namely, moon, sun, and darkness—
and the remaining ones are in the apāna.
He explains the conceptualization of these six families, beginning with "Candra" and so forth:
"Candra" is the water element; it becomes the body of the semen-element (*śukradhātu*), which is the method (*upāya*).
The light-element of wisdom becomes the sun, the fire-element, which is speech.
Even though it will be explained in this way, the meaning of wisdom and method is something else entirely:
by means of the embrace of the unequal families, through the state of being limbs of wisdom and method for the pervasive semen-element.
For the state of being a limb of wisdom occurs in skillful means (*upāya*) because, at the time of great bliss (*surata*), the mind takes on that form;
likewise, the state of being a limb of skillful means occurs in wisdom (*prajñā*).
An ill omen (*ariṣṭa*), characterized by untimely death, arises from excessive vital winds (*māruta*).
To the question "In which two bodies, above and below?", he replies:
"In the channels of body and speech, namely the *lalanā* and *rasanā*, as appropriate.
When the lower feces-channel is obstructed, then misfortune (*ariṣṭa*) occurs in the upper left channel (*vāmanāḍī*).
When the urinary channel is obstructed, death (ariṣṭa) occurs in the upper right channel;
this will be explained in detail later.
Furthermore, there is no death-sign in the channels carrying tamas and semen.
In the two channels that carry the *tamiṇī* (menstrual blood) and semen, there is birth, emergence from the womb, death, and abiding;
their own state is stability.
This is what is expressed by the words beginning with "arising" (*utpāda*), and so forth.
And regarding "at the junction of the rising of the left [nostril]":
at the junction of the transition from the left *lagna* to the right *lagna*, the *madhyamā* flows as the equinox (*viṣuva*).
He states how many inhalations and exhalations [occur]:
"Five hundred and fifty-six," and so forth:
during day and night, that is, in one full day and night consisting of twelve transitions (*saṃkrānti*), the central channel (*madhyamā*) carries six hundred and seventy-five breaths.
The left and right channels each carry twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths minus those six hundred and seventy-five.
For three years and three fortnights more than a hundred years, when the full hundred years have passed, the middle channel flows;
the left is the *vāmā*, the right is the *savyā*, and above is the *dakṣiṇā*—these are the designations for the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in sequence as the Moon, the Sun, and the Fire.
Furthermore, the *lalana* is the *iḍā*, and the other, the *rasanā*, is the *piṅgalā*.

"Having water and fire as their intrinsic nature," as before, refers respectively to Amitābha and Ratnasaṃbhava as the presiding deities of the Lotus-holder (Avalokiteśvara) and the Jewel-holder (Ratnapāṇi).

By the words "below," meaning in the *apāna*, and "the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*) and so forth," he describes the intrinsic nature [of the channels] through the movement of the two upper channels above the carriers of feces and urine.
This is the meaning:
that which is the left channel above, O virtuous one, is the central feces-channel;
that which is the right [channel] above, O virtuous one, is the left urine-carrying channel.
These two are respectively considered to be the holders of the wheel and the sword,
having the nature of Vairocana and Amoghasiddhi;
that which is above is the middle [channel].
The left channel, *sādhaḥ*, carries semen;
these too have the nature of empty cognition (*śūnyajñāna*).
Their presiding deities (*adhidaivata*) are Akṣobhya and Vajrasattva.
In the navel-lotus of the earth, there are five qualities, characterized by smell, form, taste, touch, and sound;
in the heart-lotus of water, there are four qualities, characterized by form, taste, touch, and sound;
and in the throat-lotus of fire, there are three qualities, characterized by form, touch, and sound.
In the lotus of the forehead, there is the wind element, characterized by the two qualities of touch and sound;
in the lotus of the crown, there is that of emptiness, possessing the single quality of sound.
Having grasped these, the *avadhūtī* emerges in the order of dissolution.
And by means of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and [the sequence] beginning with emptiness (*śūnya*),

it enters the earth at the navel-center. Below, from the navel, the secret place, and the jewel-lotus, the *śaṅkhinī*— which carries body, speech, and mind and consists of three, two, and one quality (*guṇa*) respectively according to the divisions of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*— emerges by way of the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
It enters through the creation [of the embryo]. This *śaṅkhinī* [channel] carries semen from the pleasure of women during sexual union;
when the menses arise during the fertile period (*ṛtu*), it carries blood.
He explains the relationship between wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*) regarding the channels of *prāṇa* and *apāna*:
"Above," and so forth.
When *prāṇa* is above, the relationship of wisdom and means exists on the left and right—that is, the left and right sides; when *apāna* is below, it is likewise.
Regarding the upward and downward flows of the *rajas* and semen:
(47) when that very [channel] which is the "bird-mouthed" (*khagamukhā*) in women carries the semen downwards, it becomes the *caṇḍālī*;
and at that same time of the menstrual cycle (*ṛtukāla*), the upper channel of women becomes the *ḍombī*.
In both cases here, women are untouchable.
However, for a man, during the menstrual period—that is, at the time of the emission of semen—she herself becomes a *ḍombī* or *avadhūtī*.
He now describes the arising of the mandalas in the left and right nostrils.
"Beginning with consciousness," and so forth.
"Beginning with consciousness" refers to the sequence of emanation, starting with space;
"beginning with earth" refers to the sequence of withdrawal.

In the middle, within the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*), the sixth circle of gnosis (*jñāna-maṇḍala*) flows, having taken from each of the five circles beginning with space eleven and a quarter breaths (*śvāsa*), thus consisting of fifty-six and a quarter breaths. Within these left, right, and central channels, there are sixty circles in the twelve-petaled navel lotus over the course of a day and night, respectively.
In the left lagna, which is odd, beginning with Aries, and in the right lagna, which is even, beginning with Taurus:
therein, when the wind flows in the right [nostril] during the Taurus lagna, then the earth-maṇḍala flows for one *daṇḍa* at the root, in the lower part of the nostril.
Likewise, on its very left side is the water-maṇḍala.
On the right side is the fire-maṇḍala;
in the upper portion is the wind-maṇḍala;
in the center is the space-maṇḍala. Thus (48).
In each of the two nostrils, one maṇḍala flows for one daṇḍa;
the meaning is that five maṇḍalas flow for five daṇḍas.
Furthermore, the phrase "beginning with earth" (bhūmyādyam) is used merely as an illustration.
The first [element], space, is also included.
To answer the question of how many breaths a single channel carries, he says:
"A nāḍikā," and so forth.
"Successively" means by way of the earth element (*kṣmā*) and so forth;
this refers to the sequence beginning with space (*ākāśa*).
Calculated by five, they become one hundred and eighty breaths.
And those [channels] carry five nāḍīs;
and by means of the twelve transits (saṃkrāntis), the one hundred and eight breaths (śvāsas) [per transit] amount, in a day and night, to twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths.
This is what is stated [in the verse beginning with] "sixty," and so forth.
He describes the rising of the ascendant in the left channel (*vāmanāḍī*).

Regarding the phrase "in the middle of the petal": when the void-mandala (*śūnyamaṇḍala*) flows through the middle of the nostril by means of Aries and so forth in the left channel, it is stated that it also flows internally in the middle of the petal.
Then, "before that" refers to the wind-mandala above and the fire-mandala on the right.
On the left is the water mandala;
"the other" refers to the earth mandala in the lower part;
"in sequence" means in the order beginning with space.
With the words "beginning with space," etc., he explains what was previously stated.
He speaks of the mutual relationship between the five maṇḍalas through the distinction of wisdom and means.
"The other" refers to the lower maṇḍala.
"In the east" refers to the upper mandala; in due order, these are earth (*dharā*) and wind (*vāyu*).
He explains the mutual relationship between these two as the cause of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*) with the words beginning "the thumb," and so forth. (49)
The thumb is the nature of earth, and the ring finger is the nature of wind;
through these two, there is the state of wisdom and means by way of the relationship between the grasped and the grasper.
For indeed, the arising of the effect occurs through union with another family (*parakula*), not through union with one's own family (*svakula*), because activity within oneself is a contradiction.
For the body-faculty arises from the earth element,
while the tactile faculty, arising from the wind element, grasps its object.
Therefore it is said:
"By means of the thumb and the ring finger," and so forth.
In this way, he states the cause for wisdom (*prajñā*) and method (*upāya*) in the right and left [hands], which are fire and water, respectively.
"The right," and so forth.
Here too, the object of taste is produced from the fire element;
the gustatory faculty, arising from the water element, perceives it.
Therefore, by means of both the middle and index fingers, there shall be the sword.
The fang-mudrā, the wing-mudrā, and the form [mudrā];
the scissors is the scissors-mudrā, which is the little finger.
These are distinct from one another.

The "union of the empty maṇḍalas" refers to the union— the oneness— of the ten maṇḍalas flowing through the left and right [channels], which is the flow of the central channel (*madhyamā*). Then, when the fingers, which possess the nature of earth and the other elements, are joined together with palms pressed against each other at the crown of the head, it becomes a single-faced vajra.
By this it is indicated:

by means of the yoga of the flow of the central channel (*madhyamā*), through the bliss of the immutable (*acyutasukha*) and the extraction of the *bodhicitta*, that [seal] is to be formed at the tip of the vajra;
that itself is the *kartarika*.
Because it consists in the cutting away of ignorance:
the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth refer to consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the rest;
the elements (*dhātu*) refer to earth (*pṛthivī*) and the rest.
The three vajras are body, speech, and mind.
Thus, they become one when [the breath] has entered the central channel.
He now describes the signs of death (ariṣṭa-lakṣaṇa).
"In the left," and so forth.
When the wind is excessive in the left or the right channel according to the sequence for one night,
due to the depletion of the *sattva* element, there will not be [rain] for one year.
Furthermore, there is another ten-day period of rain for the purpose of exhausting the dust;
then it does not blow again.
Furthermore, there is another fifteen-day period of rain until the exhaustion of the darkness.
With a twenty-day ascent, the lifespan is six months;

with a twenty-five-day ascent, the lifespan is three months. For here, the Sun, having taken up the qualities of the Moon—sound, touch, taste, form, and smell—reveals the days of misfortune (*ariṣṭa*).
Those five [increase] by five each until the fifth [house], which is the limit of increase.
Thereafter, in the sixth and seventh signs, the increase proceeds sequentially by one each;
in the seventh sign, it is the time of Pauṣṇa.

Where the cessation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) cannot be brought about by anyone whatsoever due to the entry of the fatal wind (*ariṣṭavāyu*) into the seminal element (*śukradhātu*), following that,
for the purpose of depleting the seminal element during the period of *Pauṣṇa*.
On the eighth leaf and subsequent ones, there is a sequential ascent of thirty-three days.
Here is the wheel of the twelve zodiac signs (*dvādaśarāśicakra*).

Having drawn the diagram (*puṭa*) representing the nature of ignorance and the twelve links of dependent origination upon the ground and so forth, in the first diagram, starting from the east and so on, one should [calculate] the remaining lifespan in years, months, and days, beginning with the sign of birth such as Capricorn (*makara*) and the rest, according to the division of the days of misfortune (*ariṣṭadina*).
He states the sequential arrangement as follows:
"Three, two," and so forth;
by equal years, months, six, three, two, and one.
The lifespan of embodied beings passes away by means of [the sequence] one, two, five, ten, five, and two, multiplied by one;
thus, because it follows merely as a brief indication, the second enclosure is described as the "abandonment of days.
On the previous birth-ascendant leaf, from the three-year period of one thousand and eighty days, one abandons the period of one hundred and thirty-five days starting from Capricorn.
Then, having emptied that petal, the vital power (*prāṇa-śakti*) enters the second petal, taking with it the remaining number of days.
There too, it discards three hundred and forty-five days along with the days of ascent.
Then, having emptied the second petal, the remaining days—(52)—
Having taken [the remaining days], one enters the fourth [house].
There too, one discards eighty-two days together with the days of ascent.
Then, having cleared the leaf and taken the remaining days, one enters the fifth.
There too, one abandons fifty-seven days, including the days of ascent.
Then, in the sixth [stage], one enters after taking the remaining day;
there too, one abandons twenty-eight days, including the days of ascent.
Then, having emptied the sixth, he enters the seventh;
there too, together with the days of ascent, he abandons twenty-seven days.
Having emptied the seventh and taken the remaining group of twenty-six days, he enters the eighth.
There, one abandons fifteen days.
Having rendered the eighth day empty, one takes the remaining twenty-one days and enters the ninth.
There, one abandons ten days.
Having taken the remaining eleventh day, one enters the tenth after having emptied the ninth.
Having abandoned five days in the tenth and taken the remaining day, one enters the eleventh;
therein, one abandons three days.
Then, having rendered the eleventh empty and taken the remaining three days, he enters the twelfth;
there he abandons those three days.
Having taken the remaining single day, he enters the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
Thus, through one thousand and eighty days— the number of days in three years— the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*) abandons the entire middle twelve-fold wheel of the zodiacs (*dvādaśa-rāśi-cakra*).

Thereafter, having also abandoned consciousness (*vijñāna*), the vital air (*prāṇa-vāyu*), impelled by the nature of the wheel of breath, whirls within the interval of its movement through the nostrils.
It shows the *ariṣṭa* (sign of death) in the left channel,
beginning with the words "from the base" (*mūlāt*) and so forth.

"From the base" means from the day of birth of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), according to the lunar month-counting system, by increasing by one [day] each month, through the sequence of the moon's ascent, and by the divisions of four months and fortnights.

There too, having drawn the twelve-spoked wheel as before, the day of misfortune (*ariṣṭa*) should be placed in the first enclosure, while the thirty-six months of lifespan are to be established in the second enclosure.
Then, for one month it does not flow.
At the end of the second month, when there is an increase of misfortune upon entering the third month, it flows for two days on that very same leaf.
Then, in the third month, it does not flow.
At the end of the fourth month, upon the entry into the fifth month, it flows for three days.
Thus, in six months, there are three days of *ariṣṭa*.
At the beginning of the common day (sāmānyadina), there are three [days] characterized by the Right, Left, and Unfortunate (ariṣṭa) jewels.
Thus, from thirty-six months plus the days of misfortune (ariṣṭadina), six months of life have passed.
In that leaf, the vital wind (prāṇavāyu) does not circulate.
In this way, during one day and night, it acts through eleven transitions (*saṃkrānti*).
Even when a petal is discarded, there is no decrease in the cycle of breaths consisting of twenty thousand eight hundred breaths.
(54) Then, in the second month, and again in the seventh, eighth, and ninth months, they flow for four, five, and six days respectively.
Then, after another three months of the thirty-month lifespan have passed,
it takes twenty-seven months and moves to the third leaf.
It completes one day and night through ten transitions across ten leaves.
In each month, seven, eight, and nine days flow respectively.
From twenty-seven months, three months are subtracted.
Thus, according to the stated method, one abandons the leaf of the third zodiac sign.
It performs its transition into the nine petals;
likewise, it flows for ten days, eleven days, and twelve days,
and then abandons the fourth petal.
Of the twenty-four months, three months are subtracted from the lifespan;
likewise, thirteen days and fourteen days [are subtracted].
Thereafter, it sheds the fifth leaf.
It effects the transition across seven petals.
Out of twenty-one months, three months are deficient;
likewise, it carries for sixteen, seventeen, and eighteen days respectively during those three months.
Leaving the sixth petal, it effects a transition into the six petals;
for eighteen months, three months are subtracted from the lifespan.
It flows for nineteen and twenty-one days respectively in each month.
He abandons the seventh zodiac sign and undergoes transits through five signs;
for his life, three months are subtracted from fifteen months.
In this manner, it flows for twenty-two, twenty-three, and twenty-four days respectively.
Having abandoned the eighth petal, it effects the transition (*saṃkrānti*) through four petals. Thus, three months are subtracted from the lifespan out of twelve months.
In this manner, when it flows for twenty-five, twenty-six, or twenty-seven days, it then abandons the ninth leaf.
It effects a transition across three leaves;
thus, from nine months, three months are subtracted from the lifespan.
When it flows in this manner for twenty-eight or thirty days, it then abandons the tenth petal;
it effects a transition between two petals,
whereby three months are subtracted from the lifespan out of six months.
When it flows for thirty-one days or thirty-two days, then it abandons the eleventh leaf;
it effects a transition onto a single leaf.
From three months, ninety days are subtracted from the lifespan.
Then, after having entered the first petal for three days, it flows for two days in the twelfth petal;
thereafter, it abandons the twelfth petal.
Then, it flows for one day in the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
As long as that severance of the wheel of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) occurs through the left-hand *ariṣṭa*, non-yogins go to their death.
(56) "The middle," and so forth:

when one hundred years of the time of death are complete, there is an ascent into the middle [channel] by means of even and odd days, starting from Taurus and Aries, and by the mandalas born of birth, beginning with Earth and the others.
Because of the destruction of both wings, that is, through the exhaustion of the right and left wings;
the phrase "otherwise," and so forth, is easy to understand.
He speaks for the purpose of deceiving the omens of death (*ariṣṭa*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "the signs of death" (*ariṣṭalakṣaṇam*):
one should place the vital breath (*prāṇa*), that is, the *prāṇavāyu*, at the forehead. The state of *avadhūtī* refers to the flow through the central channel (*madhyamā*).
"Otherwise," and so forth:
if that [wind] does not intensify, it does not become differentiated;
by way of the arising of the vajra, the vital wind (prāṇamāruta) does not enter the path of the avadhūtī.
Furthermore, the downward-moving wind (*apānavāyu*) does not enter the *śaṅkhinī*. To the question "What would happen then?", he says:
death results from that non-entry of those two winds, the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, into the *avadhūtī*. (57)
Or, by not entering the *śaṅkhinī*, there is indeed death. He now describes the differentiation of the joys (*ānanda*).
"Śukra," and so forth.

From the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*), the descent of the seminal essence (*śukra*) into the lotus of the *ūrṇā*—that is, the space between the eyebrows—is the first joy (*ānanda*). From there, its arrival at the throat and the heart is the second, supreme joy (*paramānanda*).

Then, following various forms of delight characterized by play, deep embraces, the sound *śītkāra*, throat-cooing, and so forth, the bodhicitta reaches the navel and the secret place; this is the third joy, the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*).
From the secret place down to the tip of the vajra-jewel, the bodhicitta remains without emission; this is the fourth joy, the innate joy (*sahajānanda*).
In that regard, non-abiding nirvāṇa exists because of the absence of both attachment and detachment in their established forms;
it is for the sake of exhausting worldly attachment.
Great passion is the Vajra-anaṅga, the immutable Lord, the sovereign throughout the three realms.
Because that state is desired by all with the wish to attain it.
Furthermore, he asks: "What, then, is established nirvāṇa?
He says: "That which [arises] from dispassion," and so forth; this is easy to understand.
He explains this very point in detail:

the moon is indeed the semen because of its immortality. Its rising occurs in the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) and the forehead; it is full [on the first day] through the divisions of the first bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth. The first lunar day (*pratipad*) is the semen, as are the second, third, fourth, and fifth days, which are characterized by these stages.
Because it has been stated merely by way of enumeration:
in the throat and the heart, there are the sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth, and the final full [digit];
in the navel and the secret place, there are the eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth, fourteenth, fifteenth, and the third full [digit].
Then, when the bodhicitta has reached the *tripūrṇā* [state] through the distinctions of *ānanda* and so forth,

the secret lotus (*guhyapadma*)— that sixteenth digit (*kalā*) which arises from supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) when the bodhicitta has reached the secret place— becomes situated at the tip of the jewel (*maṇi*) upon the head of the vajra.
Thereafter, with the arrival of the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapratipadā*), at the time of entering into detachment (*virāga*), it would be the time of emission (*cyutikāla*).
Then, from the state of detachment (*virāga*), the Sun (*ravi*) goes to the location of the *ūrṇā*.
The sixteenth digit (*kalā*) of this Sun, which has gone to the lotus of the crown (*uṣṇīṣa*), is called the "lost moon" (*naṣṭacandra*),
because it is obscured by the Sun in the form of *rajas*.
Therefore, detachment arises from the pleasure of passion;
thus, it should be abandoned.
At death, at the time of dying, for all embodied beings—gods, asuras, and humans—(60)
The nectar of the moon is the *bodhicitta*;
it moves downward by way of the path of semen.
The sun itself is the *rajas*; because it possesses the nature of *rajas*, it moves upward.
The consciousness of Rāhu is the consciousness permeated by the life-force of ignorance, characterized by existence and characterized by karma such as pleasure, pain, and so forth.
Since this is so, for this reason, the upward movement above of the lunar nectar—the white constituent—is taught;
and the downward movement below of the solar dust, which is characterized by Rāhu-consciousness, must be made into the movement toward immutable bliss.
And this demonstrates that such was the conduct of the Blessed One.

Regarding the passage beginning with "the ūrṇā," the fullness— the state of being complete— of the lunar nectar, which is the seminal essence (*śukradhātu*), occurs in the *ūrṇā*-lotus of the Buddhas.
The new moon of the sun-dust occurs in the secret place. Of those two—the full moon and the new moon—the digits belong respectively to the Buddhas in the uṣṇīṣa and the vajra-jewel.
This has been stated in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*:
"Trampling with the sole of one foot, he stands upon the surface of the earth's mandala;
trampling the peak of the universe, he stands upon the nail of his big toe.
Thus, the meaning is that the "vajra-step" is established as the "step of gnosis" (jñānapada) in its inverted form.
Furthermore, he says that such a state is "non-abiding" with the words beginning "apratiṣṭhā" (non-abiding).
The elements, such as earth and the rest, attain the state of being non-perverted and free from obscuration.
Those other elements are indivisible.

Regarding the four drops (*bindu*) of body, speech, mind, and gnosis located above the *lambikā* of the head, which are filled with imperishable bliss in successive order, he speaks of the purification of the four bodies,
beginning with "In the jewel" (*maṇau*), and so forth.
"From great bliss" means that the body-bindu which, by reversal, [descends] from the tip of the vajra, is the pure body (*śuddhakāya*) due to the exhaustion of the fourth state (*turya*).
And that [bindu] abides at the tip of the vajra.
Therefore, the mind [abides] in the jewel due to the exhaustion of deep sleep (*suṣupta*).
In the secret place, speech [is purified] through the exhaustion of the dream state;
at the navel, the body [is purified] through the exhaustion of the waking state.
And these—the dharma-body, enjoyment-body, and emanation-body—radiate forth from the pure body. (62)
Regarding the phrase "of the means" (*upāyasya*): that which is the radiation of bodies from below the tip of the vajra is the means, and for wisdom (*prajñā*), it should occur from above.
He demonstrates this with the words "on the forehead," and so forth.
Of this wisdom, the body-vajra is in the forehead as before, but inverted;
likewise, in the lotuses of the throat, heart, and navel, there are the speech-vajra, mind-vajra, and gnosis-vajra respectively.
By means of these, the emanation bodies and so forth radiate forth.
He says "karma," etc., for the purpose of increasing the bliss of the syllable (*akṣarasukha*). Now, one might object that the moon should always be in a state of increase; to this he replies:
For there can be no increase. To explain: whatever has increased must necessarily be subject to decay; otherwise, it would follow that it is eternal.
And there is no such thing as an eternal entity for which one might postulate such eternality.

Since all phenomena possess the nature of arising and ceasing, one might suspect: "Let its very nature, then, be nothing other than arising and ceasing; what is the fault in that? Anticipating this objection, he says:
"Of phenomena that lack intrinsic nature" means that for those phenomena which lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), whatever destruction or arising there may be, that is *māyā*.
For this very reason, the elements (*bhūta*) neither undergo destruction nor are they born, because they consist merely of conjunction and disjunction.
[The author] speaks of the cultivation of movement and so forth.
"By one's own wisdom," and so forth.

The mind, embraced by one's own wisdom characterized by various marks, has gone to the lotus in the secret place; that which is in the *maṇi*, the vajra-jewel, is the meditation on *spanda* (vibration) in the form of vibration within the moon.
When there is non-vibration (*niṣpandatā*) in that very jewel, that is the meditation on the unchanging (*akṣara*).
Regarding "cultivation through body, speech, and mind within the channels of body, speech, and mind"—that is, within the left, right, and central channels:
when one has entered the path of the mirage and so forth by means of the guru’s instruction, then the three channels become completely purified.

When they are thus purified, even if the vital breath (*prāṇa*) flows through the channel of the body, one must nevertheless perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*); and that is the cultivation of the body.
Thus, there is the cultivation of speech in the *vāg-nāḍī*,
and the cultivation of mind in the *madhyamā* as the *citta-nāḍī*.

When the cultivation of gnosis and the cultivation of the syllable occur in the *śaṅkhinī* and *śukra-nāḍī* respectively, then there is the synthesis, the oneness of the three vajras and the three channels.
He speaks of the binding of the four drops,
beginning with "Prajñā" and so forth.
"Melted by the passion of wisdom" means melted by the flame of Caṇḍālī.

From the forehead of the head, the "state of fullness" (*pūrṇāpada*) is the secret place; it is the ultimate bond by means of the binding of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*).
"Latent impression" (*vāsanā*) refers to an obscuration; its "removal" is its taking away. That is neither the waning nor the waxing of the full moon.

Thus, the arisen gnosis gradually attains fullness in the crown (*uṣṇīṣa*) through the stages (*bhūmi*) beginning with *muditā*, by means of the distinctions of vibration (*spanda*) and so forth. "Fullness" refers to the removal—that is, the taking away—of afflictions (*kleśa*) and the like.
It is said: "There is no cutting off of gnosis, nor is there its filling."
The mark of the moon is the moon; the moon is in the center of the moon, thus it is the "moon in the center.
Therefore, on the full moon day, the moon is not stable because it undergoes diminution at the time of its entry into the first lunar day (*pratipad*).
Likewise, the mind is unstable in the bliss of the syllable (*akṣara-sukha*).
Because it is embraced by the latent tendencies of saṃsāra, characterized by perishable pleasure and so forth,
[the mind] is not established as being full through the passion and dispassion of worldly beings; thus he says,
"In arising," and so on.

When the mind becomes motionless within the secret lotus at the moment of complete awakening (*ekakṣaṇābhisaṃbuddha*), then that mind is the *vajra*; through its non-emission (*niṣpanda*) into the *vajramaṇi*, it fulfills all moments, characterized by twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths. Thus, this mind does not abide in passion during the bright fortnight, nor does it depart into dispassion during the dark fortnight.
Therefore, situated between the two sides, it has entered into the Full Moon; it is non-dual and non-abiding.
This is stated in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*:
"Awakened in a single instant, the manifestor of all instants."
"Timeless, beyond calculation, and holding the pinnacle of the fourth dhyāna.
Thus he describes the sequence of saṃsāra,
beginning with "The uṣṇīṣa," and so forth.
From the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) of that Bodhisattva, there arises the full [moon] within the vajra-jewel.

From detachment (*virāga*), there is the waning of its digits; from the presence of the vajra, there is the accumulation of its digits. Thence follows the waning of detachment until its complete fulfillment.
Again, there is thus an arising; again, there is fullness in the jewel.
Due to dispassion, there is a loss of the digits (*kalā*), but for embodied beings, this is not a loss of knowledge.
He says that death occurs through the loss of knowledge. (66)
He explains the meaning of the word *pūrṇā*:
that which is the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) of this bodhicitta is expressed by the word *pūrṇā*.

Apart from the nature of great bliss, there is no other state characterized by sense objects and faculties, nor anything that performs creation and dissolution, nor anything characterized by arising and passing away.
This very point is clarified by the passage beginning with "bhāvāt" and so forth.
By the two solstices of one's own side, namely the white and black, which are the northern and southern [solstices].
When this immovable *bodhicitta* reaches its fullness in the secret lotus, there is fulfillment through the stages (*bhūmi*s) above.
The passage beginning with "twenty-two thousand" has its meaning already explained.

Having traversed and restrained the two sides—the left and the right—characterized by the twelve zodiac signs beginning with Aries and Taurus, one attains the twelve aspects of the reality-meaning through the acquisition of the twelve stages.
The imperishable consists of sixteen aspects because of the exhaustion of the sixteen worldly digits (*kalā*).
It is supreme non-duality because of the absence of conceptual constructions produced by the wind of karma.
That which is non-dual is "single in meaning" (*ekārtha*); that which is the dharma of non-duality is single in meaning, [as] both—(67)
Because of the absence of passion (*kṣābhāvāt*). "The great passion beginning with dispassion" refers to the fourth moment of consecration (*sekakṣaṇa*).
This is stated in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*:
"The great passion beginning with dispassion, possessing all colors, with blazing radiance."
"The Perfectly Awakened One, seated in the vajra-posture, upholds the Dharma of the Buddha’s assembly.
Thus, it is undefiled and untroubled due to the absence of both [subject and object].
This demonstrates the unity of the apprehended mind and the apprehending mind.

The word "yathā" (just as) is used for illustration. Just as the water of rivers, once entered into the ocean, attains equality with it, so too this aggregate of phenomena— consisting of both the stable and the moving— becomes equal and identical to the Immutable when it is reflected in all its aspects within that Immutable.
He states this very point again by means of an illustration:
just as this collection of elements, such as iron and the like, when consumed by mercury (*rasa*), attains the state of mercury and becomes equal to it;
or just as a collection of elements, such as earth and the like, when consumed by seeds such as those of the *kādrava* plant, attains the nature of the seed.
At the time of fruition—that is, at the time when the fruit arises—that very [reality] becomes devoid of human reckoning, meaning it is beyond calculation.

(68) In the same way, the aggregate of existents, consisting of both the stable and the mobile, when consumed by the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*) and rendered free from obscurations by the reflection of all aspects, attains the state of the supreme syllable.
The meaning is that it comes to possess the nature of all aspects.
In the analogy of the poison, he states the pervasiveness of pleasure:
"Not the bite," and so forth.
When the poison has reached its full state of pervasiveness, the one bitten no longer feels the pain of sensation at the site of the bite.
Nor does he perceive it anywhere else in any other part of the body;
nor does he perceive objects such as forms through the doors of the sense organs, such as the eyes.
Thus, when the mind has reached its full phase and attained pervasiveness, the yogi does not perceive true bliss in the *vajramaṇi*, nor elsewhere, nor objects through the doors of the sense organs.
It is stated in the *Cakrasaṃvara*:
"With hands, feet, and so forth on all sides; with eyes, heads, and faces on all sides;
possessing mindfulness everywhere in the world, it stands pervading everything."
"Even though it is situated in one place, it pervades as far as the pores and the joints of the skin.
(69) He explains this by means of the analogy of mercury and iron,
beginning with "Just as," and so forth.
In a single region, within the diamond-jewel (vajramaṇi),
[there is] that which is heated by the fire of desire and heated by the blazing of the Caṇḍālī;
"residual impressions" (vāsanā) are characterized by passion and so forth.

Just as a stone attains heat and luminosity through contact with a great gem, so too it certainly attains a state of bliss through contact with immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*). What more need be said? From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), that is, from the standpoint of absolute truth (*paramārthasatya*), what is the nature of knowledge, its power, or its conceptualization?
The meaning is that there is nothing at all to be conceptualized regarding the piercing of the mind, which is merely smeared with adventitious impurities.
This adventitious impurity does not exist within the mind;

rather, since the mind has already arisen, this [impurity] arises afterwards. For that reason, he says: it does not arise from the mind after a long interval; the meaning is that it does not arise subsequently [to the mind].
Now, since [the Buddha] was born without a mind, for that reason he said:
"He was not born without a mind.
To the question, "In what way did he abide as immutability within the mind? he replied:
"It does not abide in the mind, O Immutable One.
With the words beginning with "yadi," he investigates this very point.
These two verses are easy to understand.
In this regard, he provides an illustration using the example of copper:
if this adventitious impurity were present in the copper, then previously the copper would have been free from tarnish.
If the impurity existed for a long time and only later did the copper come into being, then from where, or by what cause, could that impurity have arisen?

If it were produced without copper, then even a sky-flower would have existence. If it remains as an indestructible entity within the copper, then it could not be removed even by an accomplished elixir (*siddharasa*).
Therefore, none of this is consistent with reason.
Therefore, this is the true meaning here:
although this blackness arises together with the copper, it perishes through contact with mercury; it does not perish later, nor earlier, nor without that [mercury].
In this way, he demonstrates the same for the mind as well.
"Like that," and so forth.
If it is asked how the word *āgantuka* is to be understood, it is said:
*āgantuka* is that which has the nature of coming (*gamanaśīla*) from all sides (*ā*).
He states that the Imperishable (akṣara) is beyond the path of speech with the words "it cannot be spoken," and so forth. In youth, during sexual union, she herself knows it.
By those who lack concentration— that is, those who lack the concentration on emptiness—
it is shown that because there is no bliss, death itself is the cause of saṃsāra.
"By those who have passed away," and so forth.
"In this way" means that the arising of detachment among sentient beings occurs according to the sequence already described;
not otherwise, and so forth.
If the arising of detachment does not occur for them, then their existence— namely, saṃsāra— cannot occur by any other means.
Therefore, the meaning is that that [detachment] alone is the cause.
"By which" means by that which is devoid of the pleasure of emission (*cyuti*).
With the words "the lustful one," and so forth, he speaks of the effort toward the pleasure of the unchanging syllable (*akṣara-sukha*).
Suffering is characterized by the fading away of passion (*rāga-virāga*).
When the substratum undergoes dissolution, there occurs the detachment of that which is supported;
thus, the connection is with the statement, "one should avoid passion for dissolution. He now describes the state of stainlessness.
Regarding the passage beginning with "akṣara" and so forth:

for the body arisen from the syllable (*akṣarodbhava-kāya*), which resides in the center of the *ūrṇā* wheel of the mind, the conjunction— that is, the merging— of the vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*) on the left and right [channels], as well as their flowing through the central channel (*madhyamā*) and the initial *hūṃ* syllable which serves as the basis for that flow through the central channel,
is not accepted.
And since this has been explained in detail by the venerable Puṇḍarīka in the *Paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*, it will not be elaborated upon here.
Now, he states the nature of dependent cause and effect,
beginning with the words "the reflection" (*bimba*), and so forth.
The image arises from the empty space as the source of all aspects...
